data.title: Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri named Morocco's first woman PM
data.description: The king of Morocco on Tuesday named Marrakesh mayor Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri the country's first woman prime minister after her centre-right Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) party won last week's parliamentary elections. El Mansouri joined the PAM in 2008 and was also the first woman to serve as mayor of Marrakesh, winning the office in 2009 before losing it six years later, then retaking it again in 2021.

data.title: Ethiopia's last Jews dream of visa for Israel
data.description: Ethiopia has one of the oldest Jewish communities in the world, rumoured to be the descendants of the Queen of Sheba and King Solomon in 950 BC. From the 1970s to 1990s, this community known as Beta Israel was persecuted under the Communist regime, and Israel evacuated more than 20,000 Ethiopian Jews in dramatic airlifts known as Operation Solomon and Operation Moses. But a few thousand were left behind.

data.title: ‘The country has become a battlefield’: Last US troops exit Iraq

data.title: Safeguards 'build a moat' around US AI firms, prevent open-source models from advancing, expert says
data.description: US President Donald Trump on Tuesday said the tech executives gathered at the White House to discuss regulating AI had signed a "morally binding" commitment to build adequate safeguards on the fast-moving technology. data.title: Inside the Ukrainian military unit training fighters from China
data.description: Despite the risks, a number of soldiers from the country seen as Russia’s biggest backer have found their way to Ukraine On the makeshift workbench in the cramped front room of a cottage near the frontlines of the Russia-Ukraine war, there are all the accoutrements of a drone workshop . The walls are lined with pliers and rolls of duct tape; the table is cluttered with screwdrivers and piles of wire. Propped up against the wall are two kamikaze drones. Only one item looks out of place in this Ukrainian village house: a pot of Chinese longjing tea, the leaves wilted from repeated top-ups. Good tea is one of the many things that Tim misses about his life in China. His parents post monthly supplies to Ukraine. “I think about all of it,” the 44-year-old said, of his home country. “It brings back memories and emotions.” Continue reading...

data.title: ‘I just saw this furry brown bottom disappear!’ In search of Samba – the fearless fugitive capybara
data.description: Six months ago, Samba made a brave, unprecedented escape from Marwell zoo. Her life on the lam continues today. We join the team hunting desperately to find her in the Hampshire countryside Samba the capybara is still at large. Along with her older sister, Tango, the intrepid rodent made her escape from Marwell zoo in Winchester in March. Tango all but gave herself up on day two; Samba broke for the marshy wetlands of the River Itchen. Word spread and within days the fugitive was an international social media star. But despite an intense search, the dense Hampshire countryside has afforded her a haven. Six months on, Samba remains elusive. Marwell’s staff still aren’t sure how the capybaras escaped, although they have their suspicions. Tango and Samba were born on Jimmy’s Farm and Wildlife Park in Suffolk in the summer of 2025. They arrived at Marwell zoo on Monday 16 March, to great excitement. “They were a little bit shy when they got here, as you would expect,” says Laura Read, the chief executive of Marwell Wildlife. “But they were fine.” They were immediately placed in a quarantined habitat, as is standard procedure for new arrivals. The plan was to keep them there for 30 days. Continue reading...

data.title: A moment that changed me: My mother fell off a mountain – and my life began again
data.description: A bad breakup had made me afraid I would be mired in anger for ever. But on that family hike, in our fear and horror as we awaited the air ambulance, my old hurts took on a different hue To steal a well-known line, 2023 is not a year on which I shall look back with undiluted pleasure. My annus horribilis began when a long-term relationship broke up in January, only six months after we had bought our first home together. I was about to turn 38 and the future I thought was mine – marriage, children – all fell apart. What followed was blow after blow: my sister announced her engagement, I was told by a fertility doctor that I was “not a suitable candidate” for egg freezing, and I soon began having multiple panic attacks a day. Ordinarily, my work would have been my solace; when I wrote, it was as if time was suspended. But now, my words abandoned me. They would not come, no matter how much I tried. So, in April, I decided to take the rest of the year off to recover. As I was self-employed, this was not a choice I made lightly – but my heart was broken and so too, it seemed, was my brain. Continue reading...

data.title: Belgium’s defence minister warns of ‘dark winter for Europe’ with more ‘hybrid warfare’ from Russia - Europe live
data.description: Theo Francken says bloc is in a ‘difficult position’ after recent increase in hybrid provocations from Moscow Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine faced “a difficult attack” from Russia overnight with “nearly 190 attack drones, as well as ballistic missiles.” “ The main target was energy infrastructure in the capital and the Kyiv region. Work is ongoing to restore electricity and water supplies everywhere they are currently unavailable.” “In the morning, a drone struck a grocery supermarket in Ivankovychi. As of now, fourteen people have been injured across the country as a result of all these strikes. Tragically, five people have been killed, including a child. ” Continue reading...

data.title: Yvette Cooper tells Labour conference ‘Sure Start’s back’ as she expands Healthy Babies programme – UK politics live

Because you had a reason to stop on every doorstep and chat to people who might not always support your party and try and get their second preference. No, it could happen with any political party. It’s whether that would be a legitimate government. I think you’ve got it completely wrong really, if you don’t mind me saying, to put it like that, because I have put out … a vision for a national care service. There are pensioners out there who watch your programme who are paying for care costs from their basic state pension. Now, is that right or fair? Continue reading...

data.title: Robbed of a childhood: how one girl in Gaza found freedom in swimming – video
data.description: Three years of war have destroyed almost every playground in Gaza. For Hala, an orphaned child, a swimming club on the beach offers a rare chance to escape the realities of war. The club was set up by Amjed Tantesh, who once hoped to train swimmers for Palestine’s Olympic team. Now, in a pool built from the rubble, he’s offering free lessons to children affected by war. The Guardian follows Hala and her brother Amir as they attend their first lesson, confront their fear of the sea and find a place where they can simply be children again Amjed Tantesh, who features in this film, has also worked as a journalist for the Guardian and other outlets. His niece, Seham Tantesh, reports for the Guardian from Gaza Continue reading...

data.title: ‘Beyond priceless’: how a halt to dredging saved the seas of Scotland’s Summer Isles
data.description: Fish and shellfish populations were falling rapidly as scallop dredgers devastated the seabed, but local activists and small-scale fishers battled hard to protect their coastline Inside a bothy overlooking the Summer Isles, in the north-west of Scotland, the lilting tones of a traditional Gaelic duo fill a room full of musicians, storytellers, artists, local people and revellers, hung with fish-shaped lanterns and “Happy Birthday” signs. It’s no ordinary birthday. The people in the small cabin have come together, on a windy night in Achiltibuie, a string of coastal hamlets and villages north of Ullapool, to celebrate an important milestone in the community’s history: a hard-won battle to protect their waters from the ravages of scallop dredging. data.title: The secret lives of men who read romance books: ‘My life is full of love, so I’m drawn to them’
data.description: It’s often assumed straight men are not interested in romantic fiction – but many are sharing their passion in forums online After a tiring day as a school maintenance worker, 28-year-old Paul loves nothing more than unwinding with a good romance novel – ideally one with a fantasy or horror element to it. He reads five or six a month – most recently Love Bytes, about an 8ft-tall werewolf woman who runs an extremely successful AI company and falls in love with a handsome ballroom instructor. Paul got into romance fiction via what he calls its “more traditional” side – such as the Regency romance series Bridgerton. He is partially sighted, so he mostly reads on his Kindle, where he can adjust the font size. In the first Bridgerton novel, “Simon, the main character, has a speech impediment that he has to work through,” says Paul. “I’m more attached to that one. Typically, I don’t come across disabled protagonists that much.” Continue reading...

data.title: On the Equality of All Things by Carlo Rovelli review – a physicist’s guide to life, the universe and everything
data.description: Near-mystical musings from a scientist who believes we are on the brink of a revolution in understanding ourselves Under the letter “B” in the index at the back of Carlo Rovelli’s latest book you will find Francis Bacon, bats, behaviourism, Henri Bergson, and the big bang. This intriguing little miscellany reflects the sweeping ambition of what is perhaps Rovelli’s most overtly philosophical work to date . Rovelli, who directs a quantum gravity research group in Marseille, has written several books on physics for the general reader, including the global bestseller Seven Brief Lessons on Physics . His latest is an attempt to integrate principles and theories from the discipline into a broader W eltanschauung : one of the essential unity of all things, and the profoundly relational and perspectival nature of the universe. “Electrons and minds, stones and laws, judgments and galaxies do not essentially differ in nature from one another,” he writes. “They are notions that illuminate each other.” Continue reading...

data.title: The Swan contestants on the most sadistic reality show on TV: ‘Ultimately, we were just a job’
data.description: In a new documentary, film-maker Erin Lee Carr lifts the lid on the 2000s TV show that shocked America It was in 2003, while listening to country radio, that Kelly first heard the casting call: “Have you dreamed about plastic surgery but never thought you could afford it?” She immediately turned up the volume. The pitch sounded too good to be true: free cosmetic procedures, a nutritionist, self-esteem work – one “life-changing opportunity” that “could transform everything”. Kristy, Cindy, Tawnya and Beth heard the call, too: the chance to overhaul oneself from the outside in, fulfilling the implicit but omnipresent promise that if you just lost a little weight and just tweaked your face a bit, your whole life would open up. You, too, could be an ugly duckling transfigured into a swan. The catch? It would all be filmed for television, of course, for a short-lived show that some have called one of the most sadistic of all time: The Swan. The Fox reality program, which ran for two seasons in 2004, brought the spectacle of intensive plastic surgery – the endurance of extreme pain and humiliation in pursuit of a narrow beauty ideal – to US living rooms with shocking bluntness: bandages and bruises, surgical cannulas pounding into flesh, curt assessments of lumps and bumps and “masculine” teeth that must be corrected in pursuit of a better you. Even among similarly thin-obsessed programs from the infamously ruthless Wild West of early reality television – America’s Next Top Model and The Biggest Loser , to name a few – The Swan stands out as especially cruel, at once hopelessly bought into punitive beauty standards on-screen and shamelessly manipulative off it. Continue reading...

data.title: Rapture review – cult Spanish horror is a deeply strange cheese dream of cinemania
data.description: Pedro Almodóvar provides a vocal cameo and his style can be traced back to this influential film This cult supernatural mystery from 1979 is a deeply strange cheese dream of a film from Spain, in which almost the entire opening 10 minutes unfolds in a jittery quiet. There are some longueurs and some pop-eyed silent-movie acting from one of its leads, yes, but also a deeply unnerving, enveloping atmosphere of dread. At least some of its fascination stems from the marginal involvement of the young Pedro Almodóvar, who did voice-overdubbing for one female character. Director Iván Zulueta was to maintain his connection with Almodóvar from then on and much of Almodóvar’s procedure can be traced back to this influential film: the rapture for movies (what a character here calls “cinemania”), the double-stranded narrative, the queer euphoria and the importance of extended flashbacks. Continue reading...

data.title: Blue Lights review – TV’s most thrilling cop show turns up the heat
data.description: This Northern Ireland-set police drama has never felt like this before … Race riots, organised crime and institutional politics bring it bang up to date Blue Lights has always been a very modern cop drama. Its tales of everyday callouts, fractious office relationships and complex long-term efforts to smash organised crime have all played out against the backdrop of post-Troubles Belfast, where lingering sectarian resentments make enforcing the law even harder than it is in the rest of austerity-era UK. But it’s never been explicitly topical: it’s never felt as if it is reading today’s national news headlines with the same appalled gaze as the rest of us. Until now. Our fourth visit to Blackthorn station pitches us and the police into a race riot. A centre offering support and resources to refugees is hosting a fete, which is a positive contribution to the area for those open to it: station sergeant and amateur baker Stevie (Martin McCann) marvels at the texture of Syrian pastry at an event that has been allocated minimal police presence. Minutes later, the whole squad has rushed to the scene to hold a line against an angry mob who want immigrants out of Northern Ireland. Bricks fly. Lives are in danger. Continue reading...

data.title: Bill Gates predicts AI will kill a billion people – but saying he’s been wrong before is quite the understatement | Arwa Mahdawi
data.description: He knows a thing or two about tech, but what to make of the views of a man who met Jeffrey Epstein 30 times and couldn’t see what a monster he was? The Bill Gates rehabilitation tour is in full swing. After having his carefully cultivated image tarnished by the revelation of his connection to Jeffrey Epstein , Gates lay low for a while. Now, however, the Microsoft co-founder is once again thrusting himself into the public consciousness, this time with a dire warning about AI . If left unchecked, AI could cause “a billion deaths”, Gates declared in an interview with NBC on Sunday. Perhaps I should be terrified by this announcement from a man who, for all his sins, knows a thing or two about technology. But I’m sick of hearing about the hypothetical dangers of AI when the technology is being used to kill people today . Gates may not be directly involved in Microsoft any more, but, rather than making prophecies about the future, I’d love to hear what he thinks about the company’s role in the AI-enabled destruction of Gaza. Continue reading...

data.title: It shouldn’t take the eviction of an 87-year-old to get Spain’s housing crisis fixed | María Ramírez
data.description: Pédro Sanchez is an admirer of Zohran Mamdani. It’s time Spanish politicians emulated the New York mayor’s relentless focus on affordable homes Maricarmen Abascal is a determined woman who uses a wheelchair to get around. She has needed her determination over the years she has spent fighting the real estate company that forced her out of her Madrid apartment last week. She had lived in the flat for more than 70 of her 87 years. Police forced their way into her apartment after a judge approved Abascal’s eviction . By then, protesters had gathered around the building, including the actor Carlos Bardem, Javier’s brother. Teargas was used against them. Abascal was taken to a Madrid hospital, suffering from anxiety and extreme exhaustion, while her supporters chanted: “You are not alone.” María Ramírez is a journalist and deputy managing editor of elDiario.es, a news outlet in Spain Continue reading...

data.title: I heard one thing loud and clear in Andy Burnham’s landmark speech: the left has won the arguments | Owen Jones
data.description: The PM’s stated trajectory is a rebuke to past Tory and Labour governments. The challenge now is to make his project progressive in word and deed As Andy Burnham delivered his conference speech to the Labour faithful yesterday, it was hard not to recall Jeremy Corbyn’s words after the party’s shattering 2019 election defeat. “I am proud that on austerity, on corporate power, on inequality and the climate emergency,” he wrote for this publication, “we have won the arguments and rewritten the terms of political debate.” Given Boris Johnson’s 80-seat majority, widespread mockery ensued. But when it comes to rhetoric, who can now deny that the left has won the argument? A Labour prime minister has declared that “Britain has been on the wrong path for a long time”, listing five villains: “Deindustrialisation, deregulation, privatisation, austerity, Brexit.” His speech was infused with class politics, as he condemned a society “run for vested interests, not in the public interest, with power held in too few hands”. Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West: How They Really Lost It, is published on 1 October. Order your copy at the Guardian bookshop Continue reading...

data.title: Prosecco pratfalls and coffee catastrophes: Neets are missing out on formative first-job experiences | Isabel Brooks
data.description: Work in the hospitality industry made me who I am. Without it, young people are denied not only an income and a step on the career ladder, but important life skills Everyone remembers their first job. More often than not, it’s in the service industry. I started at 14, pouring drinks, serving food and standing with an ice-cream tray. This is where I learned how to handle mistakes, such as dropping an entire tray of prosecco glasses, or spraying hot coffee all over a bridesmaid because I plunged the cafetiere with too much gusto. I learned how to talk to angry strangers, and what it means to have a bad manager. I learned that the customer is always right, except when you’re talking to chefs, who will throw ham at your head if you tell them that. All in all, I did 10 years of restaurant, bar, pub and cafe work, from the age of 14 to 24, and I largely attribute the formation of my character to that decade of work. But this kind of character-building experience is under threat. Job postings for temporary work in hospitality in the UK were down by 25% year-on-year between 2024 and 2025, with 22,369 fewer unique postings. Hospitality leaders have blamed rising wage and tax costs for their inability to hire new starters, and young people are bearing the brunt: nearly 1 million young people are not in education, employment or training (Neet), despite 84% of these seeking work. The Recruitment and Employment Confederation has explicitly warned that the industry relies heavily on 16- to 24-year-olds, so the impact will be on teenagers seeking their first job. In Manchester, Nell’s Pizza advertised 10 part-time roles for people between the ages of 14 and 18, and received about 2,000 applications . Isabel Brooks is a freelance writer Continue reading...

data.title: The Manchester City case shows us how the global mega-rich now expect to operate with impunity | Jonathan Liew
data.description: When transnational alliances have scarcely been weaker, the way the club was allegedly run offers a bleak vision of a world driven by brute power and wealth The cache of leaked emails and documents that would eventually lead to the crisis in which Manchester City are now embroiled was published by Der Spiegel in 2018 , and often it was the tone of the club’s communications that was as startling as their content. Of City chairman Khaldoon al-Mubarak, a trusted adviser to the royal family of the United Arab Emirates, it was said that he would “rather spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers in the world to sue [Uefa] for the next 10 years” than accept a fine. In the same tranche of documents, City lawyer Simon Cliff asserts that “Uefa doesn’t respond to anything other than aggression”, and threatens the governing body of European football – who were pursuing City over alleged financial irregularities at the time – with “the destruction of their rules and organisation”. data.title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham: grounds to hope for a better Britain | Editorial
data.description: By linking Brexit, voting reform and public services, the prime minister made a powerful, personal pitch for a brighter future Andy Burnham’s first speech as prime minister to a Labour conference was a serious attempt to argue that rebuilding the public realm will be better for the country than shrinking the state. He is right about this. Mr Burnham’s belief in the power of government is welcome, as is his instinct that by spending now on public services he will save money later. Admitting that Brexit “has done more harm than good” before setting out options for a closer relationship with the EU could be the speech’s most consequential sentence. Offering voters a bargain at the next election – give up a little of the annual triple-lock increase in pensions for free personal care for older people – is a gamble. But Mr Burnham clearly thinks that he will be able to show that enough has improved by then for him to ask voters to let him finish what he has started. The prime minister smartly recast “ take back control ” as a Labour argument. His pitch was that privatisation removed economic control, emasculating local government removed political control, and Brexit reduced control over immigration. This was deftly done – threading a common idea through housing, water, energy and Europe. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? data.translatedDescription: By linking Brexit, voting reform and public services, the prime minister made a powerful, personal pitch for a brighter future Andy Burnham’s first speech as prime minister to a Labour conference was a serious attempt to argue that rebuilding the public realm will be better for the country than shrinking the state. He is right about this. Mr Burnham’s belief in the power of government is welcome, as is his instinct that by spending now on public services he will save money later. Admitting that Brexit “has done more harm than good” before setting out options for a closer relationship with the EU could be the speech’s most consequential sentence. Offering voters a bargain at the next election – give up a little of the annual triple-lock increase in pensions for free personal care for older people – is a gamble. But Mr Burnham clearly thinks that he will be able to show that enough has improved by then for him to ask voters to let him finish what he has started. The prime minister smartly recast “ take back control ” as a Labour argument. His pitch was that privatisation removed economic control, emasculating local government removed political control, and Brexit reduced control over immigration. This was deftly done – threading a common idea through housing, water, energy and Europe. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? data.title: The Guardian view on Morocco’s election: hosting a World Cup will not placate a disillusioned generation | Editorial
data.description: A year after mass protests demanding a change in political priorities, gen Z opted out of last week’s poll en masse The spectacle of young migrants swimming en masse from Moroccan waters to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta exposed the frustration felt by a generation. One-third of the population of Morocco is aged between 15 and 30 , and more than one third of that cohort is unemployed. A dearth of opportunity at home incentivises young men in particular to take huge risks to reach the European Union. More than 100 people died in that attempted exodus, most of them by drowning. Worryingly, an adequate domestic response to a huge generational challenge is a long way off, if Morocco’s latest parliamentary election serves as any guide. In the wake of the Arab spring, democratising reforms were introduced to Morocco’s monarchical system. But a decade and a half after that supposedly transformative moment, last week’s poll laid bare an alarming collapse of trust in politics among the young. data.title: Sham City: verdict on financial breaches is damning and punishment must be severe | Jonathan Wilson
data.description: How can Manchester City be trusted under these owners after they were found to have devised £900m of ‘sham’ contracts? How bad could it be, really? How serious can a breach of arcane financial regulations be, really? Just how damning can accountancy be? Even after Friday’s revelation that Manchester City had been found guilty of all but one of the charges brought against them by the Premier League, it was perhaps difficult to grasp the scale of what that meant. After the publication of the independent commission’s findings, there can be no doubt: the commission found that Manchester City cheated, that they did so deliberately, and that they have sought to cover that up with a campaign of calculated misinformation. City continue to maintain their innocence and issued a statement insisting that “the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe”. It referred, once again, to “a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence that exists in support of all of its positions”, and, again, insisted that “the club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence”. data.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
data.description: A look at how our picks from five years ago have got on shows that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17. data.title: ‘I needed to change’: Peter O’Mahony on ditching hard-edged ritual, and his love of gardening
data.description: The former Ireland captain talks about allowing his own feelings, why every coach except Andy Farrell has been ‘a bit mad’, and pain over a ruthless exit from Munster “It’s a natural human instinct, especially as an athlete, that you don’t want to lose,” Peter O’Mahony says on a quiet evening in Dublin as a new rugby season looms over us. “But at times it got in my way and caused despair. I honestly don’t know where that deep-down hatred came from but it used to derail me at times.” The former captain of Munster, Ireland and the Lions is settling into his second year of retirement and the taciturn grit and uncompromising commitment which defined his career have been replaced by more complex reflections. O’Mahony is a fascinating character and I ask whether he would have carried the same competitive zeal if he had been a wizard at, for example, chess or mathematics. Continue reading...

Now, they are living precariously in temporary shelters For three days, Pooja Pariyal waited on the roof of Trishuli hospital with her three-month-old daughter, Ridhika. On the ground below and around the building, most of her town had been destroyed and churned into a sea of mud in the catastrophic flash floods that surged through the Himayalan border region of Nepal and Tibet in August. “Those three days were living hell for me, with no food, no working toilet and no one to help with the baby,” she says. “I had nothing to clean my baby’s soiled clothes. My milk supply had reduced because I was hungry and this poor little thing would cry her lungs out. Continue reading...

data.title: The night sky is getting 10% brighter every year. We’re forgetting what darkness feels like
data.description: If more cities start regulating outdoor lighting, we humans could make the environment better for all living creatures Every night, I can turn off the lights in my room – but I can’t do anything about the outdoor lights in the walkway or parking lot that leak through the curtains. Living in Portland, where the night is still illuminated by street lights, porch lights and parking lot glare, I forgot what it actually feels like to sleep in darkness. I was excited when I realized my travels to a residency in south-east Oregon would show me a sky I hadn’t experienced in decades. In the Oregon outback, part of the International Dark Sky Places network, I would be surrounded by 2.5m acres of unpolluted night in every direction. Continue reading...

The call from the man, in his 20s and from London, was one reason armed police were scrambled to arrest the men, who were with three vans close to the military base used by the US in its attacks on Iran. data.title: Menopause supplements costing more than £400 a year ‘no better than cheap multivitamin’
data.description: Many products aimed at women over 45 lack meaningful quantities of key nutrients, consumer watchdog Which? found Menopause supplements costing more than £400 a year are no better than a £22-a-year multivitamin, according to analysis by the consumer watchdog Which?. Which? found that many popular supplements that are aimed at women over 45 going through menopause or perimenopause lack meaningful quantities of key nutrients, yet cost 20 times more than standard multivitamins. data.title: Edinburgh joins UK universities heading for strikes as cuts spread through entire sector
data.description: Students at Edinburgh, Dundee and Nottingham face a term without any teaching as sector struggles with rising financial uncertainty Welcome classes for students at the University of Edinburgh this year didn’t focus on the lectures, seminars and essays expected. Instead, students were told about how their education was going to fit in around the strikes planned for this year, which for many will effectively wipe out a term of teaching. “This term I’ve got two courses and my dissertation. Currently, I’ve got no teaching for five weeks,” said Theo Warshaw, 22, in his final year studying geography at Edinburgh, where staff are striking over budget cuts and compulsory redundancies needed to bridge what the university’s leaders have said is a £400m shortfall. Continue reading...

data.title: As AI images become common, the threat to elections draws alarm: ‘How will voters know what’s true?’
data.description: Deepfakes and misinformation driven by artificial intelligence have become a point of deep concern for legislators, advocates and the public An image of College Park, Georgia mayor Bianca Motley Broom kissing a man – who was not her husband – in a bar spread far and wide on Facebook. The fact that it’s fake is spreading faster, now, but only after it had been seen by thousands of people. “I think this is a sad commentary about where we are in our democracy, and where we are in our political discourse,” Motley Broom said. “It also seeks to reinforce really tired stereotypes about women in leadership.” Continue reading...

data.title: It was a ghost town of three people. So how did Luckenbach rival Nashville as the heartland of country music?
data.description: In 1971, self-appointed mayor Hondo Crouch turned the Texan town into a rural respite for country stars. Soon it was immortalised in chart-topping songs – and became a symbol of a simpler American life In the summer of 1973, the US country singer Jerry Jeff Walker was in the middle of nowhere, recording his soon-to-be-classic album ¡Viva Terlingua!. A crowd was packed to the rafters in an old dancehall 70 miles west of Austin, in Luckenbach, Texas. An extension lead ran from the hall to a recording truck outside. After everyone had gone home that night, Walker stood in the street and said to Hondo Crouch, Luckenbach’s self-appointed mayor: “I wonder what we just did.” When Crouch had bought the town two years prior, its population was just three people – and according to the most recent census in 2021, it’s back at the same number. But in the 1970s, this ramshackle town thrived as Walker and his peers headed there, and Luckenbach became one of the most improbable yet important centres for country music. Continue reading...

data.title: Cotton Queen review – mystery, matriarchs and magic in pioneering Sudanese debut
data.description: Suzannah Mirghani’s first feature contains a powerful performance by Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as a village’s elder woman and tackles the long shadow of British imperialism and women’s rights ‘I decide my past,” says a village matriarch in this intriguingly political and poetic drama from Suzannah Mirghani, making her feature debut – and with it becoming the first Sudanese woman to direct a feature. (She was forced to cancel the original shoot in Sudan when war broke out in 2023 , moving production to Egypt.) It’s a film with things to say about the long shadow of the British empire, neocolonialism, women’s rights and female genital mutilation. But it mostly says it all without undermining its sense of mystery and shivers of magic realism. We’re in present day Sudan, where village elder Al-Sit (Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud) is an iron-willed woman not to be messed with. Everyone knows the story of how as a young girl she ran the British out of town; small children in the village gleefully tell the story of how she slaughtered every single last one of them. Can it possibly be true? The trauma of her past is at the centre of the film, and Mahmoud’s witchy performance, fierce and powerful, is utterly compelling. Continue reading...

data.title: Digger review – Tom Cruise’s loudmouth oil tycoon goes hard in Alejandro G Iñárritu’s eco-satire
data.description: One man’s irresponsible drilling causes a global crisis in Iñárritu’s exasperatingly laborious, self-congratulatory film A new movie from the Oscar-winning Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu is always an event. So it’s disconcerting to discover that the event in question is the most disappointing film of the year: an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire with a trick up its sleeve, featuring very good actors giving not very good performances. There are moments to enjoy in Tom Cruise’s boisterous leading turn, yes, but the film’s value resides chiefly in some dreamlike and disturbing images, distorted and bulging from the screen, conjured by cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki and production designer Dennis Gassner. An ageing, paunchy Texan oil tycoon called “Digger” Rockwell is seen fretfully getting up in the morning, cooing over his horrible old incontinent cat, taking urgent messages from underlings about a certain situation developing in his drilling station in the frozen Arctic. He is played by Tom Cruise with a wispy baldingness and various other prostheses, together with a good-ol’-boy twang and a Stetson borrowed from Slim Pickens’s bomb-riding army major in Kubrick’s Dr Strangelove. His prized possession is the battered old shovel his granddaddy used a century before, digging for black gold as a penniless young man in the lone star state. Digger likes to brandish this to make a point. Continue reading...

data.title: How Deep Is Your Love review – under the sea at Earth’s last frontier with the Psychedelic Elvis Worm
data.description: Film-maker Eleanor Mortimer accompanies a scientific expedition to the deep Pacific, where new creatures are abundant yet threatened by sea mining For the marine biologists in this whimsical eco-documentary, the answer is about 5000 metres down. In the lab, we watch them observing, describing, and classifying the bonkers-looking creatures that survive in the freezing-cold waters of the deep sea: blobby little sea pigs and alien glow-in-the-dark sea cucumbers. It seems 90% of life in the deep sea has yet to be named, explains film-maker Eleanor Mortimer in her quirky voiceover. It is the last frontier of exploration on Earth. Mortimer accompanies a team of scientists on an expedition to the eastern Pacific. It takes the ship’s robot four hours to descend the four kilometres to the ocean floor where it trundles along, grabber claw at the ready. A biologist explains that 80% of what they bring up to the surface is new to science. And one of the film’s pleasures is watching the wonderstruck awe on their faces as they clap eyes on never-before-seen creatures. The process of acquiring a Latin name for a new discovery can take years, so in the meantime scientists give them excellent temporary names like the Headless Chicken Monster and the Psychedelic Elvis Worm. Continue reading...

data.title: Dèy by Edwidge Danticat review – motherhood and trauma in Miami
data.description: The first novel in over a decade from the acclaimed Haitian-American author lacks the power of earlier works Dèy, Edwidge Danticat’s first novel in over a decade, begins with a bang. Magnolia, the daughter of Haitian parents now shopping for a birthday present for her own daughter, hears gunfire, maybe bombs, in a Miami mall. A killer is on the loose – a young man high on hate, the author of online screeds about how “our country is under attack”, obsessed by cane toads who’ve been coming in from the Amazon basin. As she scrambles to the floor of a restaurant called Oasis, surrounded by dozens of diners playing dead, a man asks, “Is this a mass grave?” Things have always been tough for Magnolia. Her mother chases pigeons by day, sleepwalks at night, is on and off lithium. Her father worked for many years as a bus driver in Brooklyn, saving every cent so he could buy a nice retirement home back in Haiti. She was brought up by an “aunt” whose family had been killed by goons employed by Haiti’s dictator-in-chief Papa Doc Duvalier. Later she gets to college, where “school was my refuge”. Continue reading...

data.title: ‘Delays are always welcome’: 10 of the best railway station pubs in England
data.description: Converted from Victorian buffet bars, ticket offices and waiting rooms, these station pubs offer beautifully restored interiors, real ales and a slice of railway history No prizes for guessing what this pub used to be… The Old Ticket Office has high ceilings, walls painted shades of locomotive green and booths resembling train carriages; there are outdoor tables on Station Square. A live train departures board theoretically prevents passengers lingering too long, and a canning machine means any draught beer is also available to take away (the hatch on platform 4 also does takeaway orders). There are five handpulls plus Young’s usual spritz menu and other drinks, plus light bites and pizzas. The pub is currently closed for roof repairs and expected to reopen by the end of October. data.title: Cullen skink pies, vegetarian haggis and chippy fritters: Ali Stoner’s recipes for twists on Scottish classics
data.description: Scots have a rich food history that’s been passed down through generations. Here are my modern takes on traditional Celtic staples There is a depth and history to Scotland’s food that reaches far beyond deep-fried Mars bars or urban myths about haggis. Kitchens were humble and full of life – recipes passed by word of mouth, scraps of paper shared between friends, generations stitching together simple meals. I’m lucky enough that my mum taught me how a potato, a handful of oatmeal and a bit of salt and butter could make a meal and hold a story, but life changes – new ingredients arrive, we move away, time grows shorter – and, sometimes, those simple, comforting recipes drift out of reach. Today’s dishes began as a keepsake for my children – to save old recipes, to record a feeling of home – but also as an invitation to discover what happens when memory meets invention. Continue reading...

data.title: Sali Hughes on beauty: a buzzy new brand is aimed at women over 40 – and the industry is taking notice
data.description: Beauty mogul Sarah Creal decided there was too much emphasis on the teen market – so she designed a range of products for older women. Now others are following suit It’s rare that I devote a whole column to one brand, but not as rare as the decision by any beauty company to back women over 40, so I think Sarah Creal is worthy of the inches. Creal, co-creator of Victoria Beckham Beauty and product developer of countless global companies for more than 30 years, felt that women of her generation (she’s 56) and their specific beauty challenges (hooded eyelids, decreased product wear time and so on) were being overlooked by major brands in favour of teenagers. Wander into any lip-oil slicked, Korean sheet-mask filled, freckle-pen-dotted branch of Sephora and tell me she’s wrong. Continue reading...

Now others are following suit It’s rare that I devote a whole column to one brand, but not as rare as the decision by any beauty company to back women over 40, so I think Sarah Creal is worthy of the inches. Creal, co-creator of Victoria Beckham Beauty and product developer of countless global companies for more than 30 years, felt that women of her generation (she’s 56) and their specific beauty challenges (hooded eyelids, decreased product wear time and so on) were being overlooked by major brands in favour of teenagers. Wander into any lip-oil slicked, Korean sheet-mask filled, freckle-pen-dotted branch of Sephora and tell me she’s wrong. Continue reading...

data.title: Jonathan Anderson mixes Austen romance with chic streetware in Dior’s Paris show
data.description: Designer’s latest work takes bold steps away from the fashion house’s brand, creating a show that felt like an event “I want to land on a vibe.” This was how Dior designer Jonathan Anderson, one year into what is arguably the biggest job in fashion, summed up his assignment before his latest show. Expounding on chiffon and buttons with the intensity of a barrister delivering a closing speech in the high court, ruffling his hair as if his mind might at any moment explode with ideas, Anderson brings more brainpower to the pursuit of the vibe than the superficial phrasing suggests. The vibe is coming in to land. This Dior show felt like an event, which is the bar Christian Dior set for his successors back in 1947, when his New Look silhouette made front pages all over the world. Overnight, trees had emerged out of the circular pond in the Tuileries Garden in Paris, and – thanks to the deep pockets of owners LVMH – a magical mist conjured to swirl around them, lending a cinematic grandeur to the slender catwalk spanning the water. (The trees will be replanted elsewhere in the gardens, after the show.) Continue reading...

data.title: Donald Trump's Maga cult is finally crumbling | Arwa Mahdawi
data.description: With the midterms looming, and after the Epstein files and the war on Iran, Trump superfans are losing faith in their lame duck president It took a dead child sex offender and a disastrous war to do it, but it looks as though the Maga faithful are slowly beginning to lose confidence in dear leader. As Donald Trump’s approval ratings drop to record lows, some of his most fervent supporters are turning on him. See, as exhibit one, Trisha Hope, who was once a proud member of the Front Row Joes, a group of Trump superfans who follow the president to rallies around the country. They have custom-made T-shirts ! They have branded baseball caps! They even have the attention of Trump himself, who frequently shouts out the group. He did once accidentally call them the “ front row Jacks and Joes ”, but who can expect a man of his calibre to pay attention to the plebs, eh? Continue reading...

data.title: 4-winged fossil found in Liaoning challenges single origin of dinosaur flight
data.description:

The newly discovered species, named Norellraptor barsboldi, is a four-winged predatory dinosaur measuring 57cm (22 inches) long.

data.title: Evangélicos votam à direita mesmo sem indicação de candidato na igreja

data.title: Insändare. Fokusera mer på likheter

data.title: Kaptenen och lotsen döms efter Tjörnolyckan
data.description: Båtsemestern slutade i tragedi när en fritidsbåt blev påkörd av ett fraktfartyg utanför Tjörn. Kaptenen och lotsen åtalades för vållande till annans död, vållande till kroppsskada och vårdslöshet i sjötrafik. Nu döms de på alla tre punkter och påföljden blir villkorlig dom. ”Kollisionen hade kunnat undvikas”, skriver rätten.

data.title: Gamla kontor tappar när företagen väljer nytt och centralt
data.description: Mediankontoret har krympt från 225 till 190 kvadratmeter sedan i början av 2000-talet, enligt en ny rapport från Newsec. Företag efterfrågar moderna lokaler i attraktiva lägen medan ”gammelkontoren” kämpar i allt större motvind. – Kontoret är en mötesplats snarare än en arbetsplats, säger Max Barclay, vd på Newsec.

data.title: DN Debatt. ”Om AI bygger programvaran – vem bygger då Sverige?”
data.description: DN DEBATT. AI-utvecklingen går blixtrande snabbt. I dag ser vi två parallella spår: Å ena sidan används AI allt mer i praktiken, men i skymundan. Å andra sidan fortsätter många organisationer att agera som om digital förändring bara händer andra. Historien visar att varje stort teknikskifte öppnar ett fönster. Frågan är vad Sverige gör nu, skriver fem it-experter.

data.title: Copernicus: bijna helft Europese bevolking dit jaar blootgesteld aan te hoge ozonwaarden
data.description: Ongeveer de helft van de Europese bevolking heeft dit jaar al lucht ingeademd waarvan de ozonwaarden „slecht” tot „extreem slecht” waren. Ozon kan diep doordringen in de luchtwegen en hoesten, branderige ogen en kortademigheid veroorzaken. Ook kan het astma-aanvallen en klachten van mensen met luchtwegaandoeningen verergeren.

data.title: Francja tonie w długach. Druga gospodarka strefy euro stała się „słabym ogniwem”
data.description: Finanse publiczne Francji są w najgorszym stanie od czasów odbudowy po II wojnie światowej. Jak donoszą czołowe dzienniki „Le Figaro” i „Le Monde”, dług publiczny kraju przebił barierę 119 proc. PKB. Paryż stracił zaufanie rynków finansowych i pożycza dziś pieniądze na gorszych warunkach niż Włochy czy zadłużona Grecja. Na katastrofalny koktajl ekonomiczny składają się niemal zerowy wzrost gospodarczy, kryzys energetyczny oraz strach inwestorów przed przejęciem Pałacu Elizejskiego przez Marine Le Pen w maju 2027 roku.

data.title: Turek na radu ministrů pro životní prostředí EU nepojede. Poprvé vyrazí Červený
data.description: Poslanec za Motoristy Filip Turek nepojede na Radu ministrů pro životní prostředí, která se koná 12. října v Lucemburku. Poprvé na jednání, kde se má také hlasovat, vyrazí ministr životního prostředí Igor Červený. Právě ministr v minulosti uvedl, že pokud se bude jednání v EU týkat spalovacích motorů či Green Dealu, bude tam často jezdit právě Turek. Ten však nyní čelí vyšetřování kvůli dopravní nehodě a dočasně se kvůli ní vzdal funkce zmocněnce pro Green Deal.

data.title: Hušbauer nevyloučil povolební spolupráci s ODS. Scheinherrovi vadí „spící“ primátor
data.description: Nedostupné bydlení zůstává jedním z hlavních problémů Prahy. Budoucí vedení metropole však bude muset řešit i mnoho dalších výzev, například v oblasti dopravy. data.title: Horor na letu do Izraele. Pilot chtěl havarovat, cestující ho pomohli přemoct

Tomu zabránil druhý pilot s pomocí skupiny pasažérů.

data.title: Muzeum Dinosauria v Praze oslaví pět let. Poprvé ukáže novou kostru Tenontosaura
data.description: Dinosauria Museum Prague, které se nachází nedaleko ruzyňského letiště, oslaví v sobotu 3. října pět let od svého otevření. Při této příležitosti návštěvníkům poprvé představí novou kostru Tenontosaura, která je ze 75 procent původní. Muzeum také rozšířilo expozici ptakoještěrů a připravilo přednášky a komentované prohlídky. Po celý den nabídne zvýhodněné vstupné.

data.title: Do školy se po epidemii salmonelózy vrátila jen polovina žáků. Obědy budou dovážet
data.description: Žáci Masarykovy základní školy v pražském Újezdu nad Lesy se po několika dnech ředitelského volna vrátili zpět do lavic. Děje se tak poté, co stovky strávníků onemocněly po konzumaci prošlých vajec, ze kterých se ve školní jídelně připravovaly uhlířské špagety. Ředitel školy Libor Skala uvedl, že ve škole dál pokračují ve zvýšené míře hygienická opatření. Do školy ve čtvrtek přišla o něco víc než polovina všech žáků a polovina celkového počtu učitelů.

data.title: Jsem frajer, smál se řidič s téměř 4 promile. Spolujezdkyně kopla do auta policie
data.description: Na první pohled bylo jasné, že dvojice, která v Dubňanech na Hodonínsku vystoupila z auta a ptala se na cestu, není ve stavu, kdy mohla usednout za volant. Když ji na to svědci upozornili, muž se ženou se jejich varování vysmáli, nasedli do Škody Felicie a pokračovali v jízdě. Policisté je zanedlouho zastavili. Řidič při opakované dechové zkoušce nadýchal 3,88 promile. Dvojice pak skončila v poutech a policejní cele.

data.title: Třímetrový orloj z kostek oživí prodejnu Lego v Praze. V Kladně vznikal 1 980 hodin
data.description: Třímetrový pražský orloj ze stavebnice Lego, který vznikal v Kladně, se na podzim představí návštěvníkům nové prodejny v ulici Na Příkopě v Praze. data.title: Ač se to někomu nelíbí, je správné zklidňovat provoz, říká lídr STAN v Plzni
data.description: Aleš Tolar, náměstek primátora pro dopravu a životní prostředí, jde po čtyřech letech do komunálních voleb v Plzni znovu jako lídr hnutí STAN. Kromě toho, že je ve vedení města, je také starostou městského obvodu Plzeň-Malesice. „Doprava ve městě nemá být souboj, zda auta, nebo MHD, nebo cyklisté, či pěší. Musí to být vyvážený mix všeho. A sdílená zóna na Americké takovým vyváženým mixem je,“ říká Tolar.

data.title: Ranní snímek z družice potěšil meteorology. Česko je celé růžové

data.title: Nikdo se jí nedotkne! Horkou fázi brazilské kampaně ovládl spor o Pannu Marii
data.description: Brazilská svatá patronka Panna Marie z Aparecidy se stala motivem sváru v kampani před prezidentskými volbami, která se s blížícím nedělním prvním kolem dostala v Brazílii do horké fáze. Jeden z favoritů volby Flávio Bolsonaro totiž musel odmítnout zvěsti, že by Panně Marie odebral při vítězství ve volbách titul patronky této latinskoamerické země. Naopak současný prezident Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva garantoval, že na takový krok nemá ani pomyšlení. Oba politici vyzvali k náboženské toleranci.

data.title: Budu hlasovat podle selského rozumu, řekla Kuchařová. Nové členy rady kritizuje i Malá
data.description: Noví členové Rady vlády pro lidská práva ve středu poprvé usedli k jednání. Jejich jmenování v posledních dnech kritizovaly lidskoprávní organizace, podle nichž jsou některé jejich postoje v rozporu s posláním rady. Právník spojený s protipotratovým Hnutím pro život Jakub Kříž kritiku odmítá a svou kvalifikaci opírá o dvacet let praxe. „Kontroverzní, ale respektuji,“ zhodnotila výběr vládní zmocněnkyně pro lidská práva Taťána Malá.

Principalmente têm aumentado a presença de ozono ao nível do solo (troposférico).  Por exemplo, metade da população europeia já esteve exposta, este ano, a níveis maus ou extremamente maus de ozono.

data.title: Poluição atravessa continentes e percorre milhares de quilómetros
data.description: Nos primeiros oito meses, o ano de 2026 fica marcado pela força com que a poluição atravessou continentes. O relatório Atmosphere Watch conclui que "o fumo dos incêndios florestais, o pó do deserto e outras formas de poluição atmosférica nociva para a saúde percorreram, por vezes, milhares de quilómetros."

data.title: Le jour où Intwari faillit faire tomber un géant
data.description:
Bujumbura n'était pas un stade ce mardi 29 septembre 2026. C'était un chaudron. Un ventre bouillant où un public nombreux était venu défier la logique. 
 Car, sur le papier, l'affiche n'avait rien d'équitable. D'un côté, l'Algérie, l'ogre, le mondialiste, l'armada verte venue du nord avec ses étoiles et son histoire. De l'autre, le Burundi, blessé par Lomé, dos au mur, que personne n'attendait. 
 Et pourtant.

data.title: Jean-Jacques Nyenimigabo s’en est allé
data.description:
C’est après une longue maladie que cet ancien professeur de feu Pierre Nkurunziza, un chef de l’Etat qu’il a servi en tant qu’ami personnel, ministre et conseiller, il l’a rejoint ce mardi 29 septembre 2026. 
Dans son Edition spéciale de 2010 consacrée à 50 personnalités qui faisaient avancer le pays, le journal Iwacu lui avait consacré une page dans ses colonnes.  
« Le ministre jeune des Sports et de la Culture », tel était le titre.

data.title: Projets communaux : miser sur l’emploi pour réduire le chômage des jeunes
data.description: Face au chômage persistant des jeunes, les communes sont appelées à privilégier des projets durables et adaptés aux potentialités locales. Un montant de 944 milliards de BIF est prévu pour les communes dans l’actuelle année budgétaire. Agriculture, élevage, transformation agroalimentaire ou encore unités de production : les initiatives discutées lors d’une conférence-débat à Gitega montrent les possibilités de création d’emplois ainsi que la nécessité de mieux étudier les projets avant leur financement.

data.title: Alessandro Villa présente ses lettres de créance au président Ndayishimiye
data.description:
L’ambassadeur de l’Union européenne au Burundi, S.E. M. Alessandro Villa, a officiellement présenté ses lettres de créance au président de la République du Burundi, Évariste Ndayishimiye ce 29 septembre 2026. Cette cérémonie marque le début officiel de sa mission diplomatique au Burundi, deux semaines après la remise des copies figurées de ses lettres de créance au ministre des Affaires étrangères, Édouard Bizimana. 
Par Jules Bercy Igiraneza

data.title: Droit à l’information : la CDHC sonne l’alerte sur les deepfakes et le désordre informationnel au Cameroun
data.description: © DR Dans une déclaration de 13 pages signée le 30 septembre 2026 à Yaoundé par son président James Mouangue Kobila, la Commission des Droits de l'Homme du Cameroun (Cdhc) fait le bilan à l’occasion de la journée internationale de l'accès universel à l'information. Elle salue les efforts du Mindef et du Mincom contre les fake news, mais s'inquiète de la montée des deepfakes et du silence de certaines administrations. Chaque 28 septembre, le monde célèbre la Journée internationale de l'accès universel à l'information (JIAUI). Pour 2026, le thème retenu est : "Préserver l'intégrité de l'information à l'ère numérique : le rôle de l'accès à l'information face au désordre informationnel". Dans sa déclaration annuelle, la Cdhc rappelle que cette journée est née en 2002 à Sofia, proclamée Journée africaine en 2012, puis Journée internationale par l'UNESCO en 2015 et par l'ONU en 2019. Pour la Commission, l'accès à l'information est un "droit-racine" qui permet d'exercer tous les autres droits. Ce que la Cdhc salue en 2026 La Commission salue les efforts des pouvoirs publics et de leurs partenaires pour favoriser une information fiable. Il s’agit des Forces de défense face à la cyber-désinformation. A ce sue, la commission fait référence au communique de la Défense du 4 septembre 2026 qui dément un faux communiqué sur les résultats des concours de la Gendarmerie, et celui du 10 juin 2026 qui dément une rumeur virale sur un prétendu commerce de chair humaine à Yaoundé. C’est aussi le cas du Conseil national de la communication (CNC) dans sa décision du 13 août 2026. Laquelle suspend de trois mois, puis de six mois M. Martial Owona et avertissant le directeur de Vision 4 pour des propos tenus le 2 juin 2026 et jugés attentatoires à la dignité de Me Félicité Esther ZEIFMAN. Une décision récente du CNC suspend la chaine, sanctionne trois journalises du Groupe l’Anecdote. Dans le même sillage, la commission liste le ministre de la Communication qui a publié une mise au point le 30 juin 2026 pour neutraliser un faux décret nommant un vice-président de la République ; L'Unesco qui a organisé un séminaire le 5 mai 2026 à Yaoundé pour former les lanceurs d'alerte et créateurs de contenus à la communication responsable, et l'atelier du 9 février 2026 à Yaoundé 3 sur l'éducation aux médias et à l'IA (EMA-IA) pour 200 jeunes. Sans oublier le Minpostel qui a lancé le programme PATNUC le 21 septembre 2026 pour former 15 000 agents publics à la transformation numérique, et le projet InReach pour l'accessibilité des sourds à l'information. Cependant, malgré ces efforts, la commission exprime ses craintes. Les six grandes inquiétudes de la Commission La commission demeure préoccupée par la circulation récurrente de contenus faux ou manipulés, qui affecte la confiance dans les sources ; les risques liés à l'IA générative, notamment la production de deepfakes audio et vidéos qui rendent difficile la vérification de l'authenticité ; le fait que plusieurs administrations ne publient pas de manière proactive les informations d'intérêt public. Leur réticence crée un "vide informationnel qui alimente spéculations et propagation de rumeurs" ; la persistance des disparités territoriales : pas de connexion internet fiable et abordable en zones rurales ; la fragilité économique des médias locaux : coûts de production en hausse, précarité structurelle qui anéantit les capacités d'investigation ; le coût élevé des forfaits data mobiles, obstacle pour les ménages à faibles revenus. La CDHC recommande pour améliorer Rappelant que sur les 220 recommandations acceptées par le Cameroun lors de l'Examen Périodique Universel (EPU) le 26 mars 2024, deux concernent l'accès à l'information, la Commission recommande au Mincom de finaliser le cadre législatif général sur l'accès universel à l'information et le soumettre au Parlement, avec des procédures d'accès claires et des voies de recours effectives. Au Minpostel, Mincom, ANTIC et Minjustice la commission recommande d’élaborer un cadre national pour un usage responsable de l'IA générative, avec des mécanismes de détection des hypertruquages. Elle recommande aussi aux institutions concernées d’intégrer des modules d'éducation aux médias et à la vérification des faits dans les programmes scolaires, comme déjà expérimenté en Algérie, Kenya et Nigéria ; de renforcer la coordination pour améliorer l'accès à l'électricité, la couverture réseaux et l'accessibilité économique d'Internet, particulièrement en zones rurales ; de s'approprier les outils d'éducation au numérique et systématiser le recoupement des sources avant toute diffusion ; Aux utilisateurs des réseaux sociaux, elle demande d’adopter des pratiques cybercitoyennes responsables, en substituant "à la culture du partage instantané celle de la vérification de l'authenticité, afin de tarir collectivement les flux de désinformation". La Cdhc marque ainsi sa contribution pour améliorer l’accès à l’information, dans un pas où les journalistes sont encore à certains espaces interdis d’accès pour collecter les données. data.translatedTitle: Droit à l’information : la CDHC sonne l’alerte sur les deepfakes et le désordre informationnel au Cameroun
data.translatedDescription: © DR Dans une déclaration de 13 pages signée le 30 septembre 2026 à Yaoundé par son président James Mouangue Kobila, la Commission des Droits de l'Homme du Cameroun (Cdhc) fait le bilan à l’occasion de la journée internationale de l'accès universel à l'information. Elle salue les efforts du Mindef et du Mincom contre les fake news, mais s'inquiète de la montée des deepfakes et du silence de certaines administrations. Chaque 28 septembre, le monde célèbre la Journée internationale de l'accès universel à l'information (JIAUI). Pour 2026, le thème retenu est : "Préserver l'intégrité de l'information à l'ère numérique : le rôle de l'accès à l'information face au désordre informationnel". Dans sa déclaration annuelle, la Cdhc rappelle que cette journée est née en 2002 à Sofia, proclamée Journée africaine en 2012, puis Journée internationale par l'UNESCO en 2015 et par l'ONU en 2019. Pour la Commission, l'accès à l'information est un "droit-racine" qui permet d'exercer tous les autres droits. Ce que la Cdhc salue en 2026 La Commission salue les efforts des pouvoirs publics et de leurs partenaires pour favoriser une information fiable. Il s’agit des Forces de défense face à la cyber-désinformation. A ce sue, la commission fait référence au communique de la Défense du 4 septembre 2026 qui dément un faux communiqué sur les résultats des concours de la Gendarmerie, et celui du 10 juin 2026 qui dément une rumeur virale sur un prétendu commerce de chair humaine à Yaoundé. C’est aussi le cas du Conseil national de la communication (CNC) dans sa décision du 13 août 2026. Laquelle suspend de trois mois, puis de six mois M. Martial Owona et avertissant le directeur de Vision 4 pour des propos tenus le 2 juin 2026 et jugés attentatoires à la dignité de Me Félicité Esther ZEIFMAN. Une décision récente du CNC suspend la chaine, sanctionne trois journalises du Groupe l’Anecdote. Dans le même sillage, la commission liste le ministre de la Communication qui a publié une mise au point le 30 juin 2026 pour neutraliser un faux décret nommant un vice-président de la République ; L'Unesco qui a organisé un séminaire le 5 mai 2026 à Yaoundé pour former les lanceurs d'alerte et créateurs de contenus à la communication responsable, et l'atelier du 9 février 2026 à Yaoundé 3 sur l'éducation aux médias et à l'IA (EMA-IA) pour 200 jeunes. Sans oublier le Minpostel qui a lancé le programme PATNUC le 21 septembre 2026 pour former 15 000 agents publics à la transformation numérique, et le projet InReach pour l'accessibilité des sourds à l'information. Cependant, malgré ces efforts, la commission exprime ses craintes. Les six grandes inquiétudes de la Commission La commission demeure préoccupée par la circulation récurrente de contenus faux ou manipulés, qui affecte la confiance dans les sources ; les risques liés à l'IA générative, notamment la production de deepfakes audio et vidéos qui rendent difficile la vérification de l'authenticité ; le fait que plusieurs administrations ne publient pas de manière proactive les informations d'intérêt public. Leur réticence crée un "vide informationnel qui alimente spéculations et propagation de rumeurs" ; la persistance des disparités territoriales : pas de connexion internet fiable et abordable en zones rurales ; la fragilité économique des médias locaux : coûts de production en hausse, précarité structurelle qui anéantit les capacités d'investigation ; le coût élevé des forfaits data mobiles, obstacle pour les ménages à faibles revenus. La CDHC recommande pour améliorer Rappelant que sur les 220 recommandations acceptées par le Cameroun lors de l'Examen Périodique Universel (EPU) le 26 mars 2024, deux concernent l'accès à l'information, la Commission recommande au Mincom de finaliser le cadre législatif général sur l'accès universel à l'information et le soumettre au Parlement, avec des procédures d'accès claires et des voies de recours effectives. Au Minpostel, Mincom, ANTIC et Minjustice la commission recommande d’élaborer un cadre national pour un usage responsable de l'IA générative, avec des mécanismes de détection des hypertruquages. Elle recommande aussi aux institutions concernées d’intégrer des modules d'éducation aux médias et à la vérification des faits dans les programmes scolaires, comme déjà expérimenté en Algérie, Kenya et Nigéria ; de renforcer la coordination pour améliorer l'accès à l'électricité, la couverture réseaux et l'accessibilité économique d'Internet, particulièrement en zones rurales ; de s'approprier les outils d'éducation au numérique et systématiser le recoupement des sources avant toute diffusion ; Aux utilisateurs des réseaux sociaux, elle demande d’adopter des pratiques cybercitoyennes responsables, en substituant "à la culture du partage instantané celle de la vérification de l'authenticité, afin de tarir collectivement les flux de désinformation". La Cdhc marque ainsi sa contribution pour améliorer l’accès à l’information, dans un pas où les journalistes sont encore à certains espaces interdis d’accès pour collecter les données. data.title: Bassin du Lac Tchad : les survivants de Boko Haram refusent de céder
data.description: © . Dans son ouvrage intitulé « Violentées, pas anéanties », Ramat Abadjida raconte celles et ceux que Boko Haram a meurtris, mais pas réduits au silence. Femmes, jeunes et hommes témoignent d’une résilience quotidienne, entre survie, reconstruction et dignité. Il y a les cartes de la guerre, les bilans humanitaires, les statistiques des déplacements forcés. Et puis il y a les vies derrière les chiffres. C’est ce que cherche à retrouver Ramat Abadjida dans « Violentées, pas anéanties : la résilience des populations affectées par Boko Haram dans le bassin du Lac Tchad », publié chez Guiguess Éditions. Son ouvrage s’intéresse à un territoire frappé depuis plus d’une décennie par les violences de Boko Haram, le bassin du Lac Tchad, espace transfrontalier partagé entre plusieurs pays, où des millions de personnes ont vu leur quotidien basculer. Loin d’un récit uniquement consacré aux destructions, l’auteur choisit de regarder ce qui demeure. Dans les villages abandonnés, dans les camps de déplacés, dans les communautés dispersées par la peur, il observe les gestes simples qui permettent de continuer à vivre. Entre autres reconstruire une activité économique, maintenir des solidarités familiales, protéger les enfants, préserver une identité collective. La résilience est le fil conducteur de l’ouvrage. Mais Ramat Abadjida refuse d’en faire un synonyme de soumission ou d’acceptation silencieuse de la souffrance. Pour lui, elle représente « une forme d’intelligence sociale, une capacité des populations à s’adapter sans renoncer à leur dignité ». Survivre devient alors une manière de résister. Dans le chapitre consacré aux déplacés internes et aux réfugiés, l’auteur décrit une réalité brutale, celle de familles contraintes de fuir en quelques heures, sans préparation, sans ressources, parfois sans destination précise. « Lorsque les violences de Boko Haram forcent des milliers de personnes à fuir leurs villages, ces déplacés internes n’ont souvent que très peu de temps pour s’organiser », écrit-il. Les camps apparaissent alors dans l’urgence, autour de zones considérées comme « plus sûres », mais où l’incertitude reste omniprésente. Derrière cette crise humanitaire, le livre insiste sur les trajectoires individuelles. Les déplacés ne sont pas seulement des personnes déracinées, ce sont aussi des femmes qui reprennent une activité pour nourrir leur famille, des jeunes qui cherchent à reconstruire un avenir, des communautés qui réinventent des formes d’entraide dans des conditions extrêmes. Les femmes occupent une place centrale dans cette chronique de la survie. Souvent exposées aux violences et aux pertes, elles deviennent aussi des figures essentielles de la continuité sociale. Selon l’auteur, « elles sont parmi les premières à s’adapter à la nouvelle réalité économique provoquée par la destruction des infrastructures et la disparition des moyens de subsistance ». Dans les espaces de déplacement, elles organisent, entreprennent, transmettent et maintiennent les liens qui empêchent les communautés de se décomposer. Ramat Abadjida propose à travers quinze chapitres et 130 pages, une lecture globale d’une crise où se croisent enjeux sécuritaires, urgences humanitaires et transformations sociales. Expert en paix et sécurité, spécialiste des dynamiques du bassin du Lac Tchad, il a mobilisé son parcours académique (master en paix et sécurité, master en études internationales et stratégiques, MBA en management des organisations) pour articuler analyse stratégique et approche humaine. Cet article Bassin du Lac Tchad : les survivants de Boko Haram refusent de céder est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Cameroun-MRC : le récépissé du 28 septembre délivré, Willy Mengue tente de faire annuler la convention du 17 octobre
data.description: © DR Le parti de Maurice Kamto a obtenu le récépissé pour sa convention extraordinaire. Au lendemain de cette délivrance, l'ex-militant Willy Mengue a saisi le Sous-préfet pour réclamer son interdiction. Une offensive que démonte point par point Maître Sikati. C'est un tournant après dix mois de blocage administratif. Le Mouvement pour la renaissance du Cameroun peut à nouveau tenir une réunion publique. La preuve, le sous-préfet de Yaoundé IV a délivré le récépissé le 28 septembre 2026 prenant acte de la déclaration de réunion publique déposée le 23 septembre par Roger Justin Noah, secrétaire général adjoint n°1 du MRC. Objet : convention extraordinaire le samedi 17 octobre 2026, de 08h à 20h, au siège d'Odza. Mais 24 heures plus tard, la contre-offensive est lancée. Willy Mengue, membre exclu et contestataire de son exclusion, saisit le même sous-préfet qui a délivré le récépissé. Objet : "Signalement de tensions internes et de risques de troubles à l'ordre public à l'occasion de la Convention nationale du MRC annoncée pour le 17 octobre 2026". Se présentant comme membre du parti, conseiller régional Centre 1 et ancien membre du directoire du MRC, il demande à l’autorité administrative d’interdire la tenue de la convention pour ce motif-là. Il s’adosse sur l’affaire qui l’oppose au parti et pour laquelle il vient de saisir la Cour d’appel du Centre après une première décision rendue au tribunal de première instance d’Ekounou. Sur la base de ces éléments, maître Sikati, cadre, conseil du MRC a réagi à travers une tribune libre. Selon lui, la démarche de M. Mengue ne peut prospérer. En trois points, il tente de déconstruire son raisonnement. Comme premier point saillant soulevé par l'avocat : l'appel n'est pas suspensif. Il rappelle qu'en matière de référé, les articles 189 et 191 du Code de procédure civile et commerciale sont clairs. Le recours introduit le 20 septembre contre l'ordonnance du 17 septembre ne suspend pas les effets de cette ordonnance. Le récépissé du 28 septembre reste donc pleinement valable jusqu'à une éventuelle infirmation par la Cour d'Appel. En deuxième point il invoque le défaut de qualité. Pour maître Sikati, Willy Mengue ayant été exclu du MRC, il n'a plus qualité pour contester la vie interne du parti. Son signalement au Sous-préfet relèverait dès lors d'une démarche personnelle et non d'un militant habilité. En troisième point, l’avocat martèle que le récépissé fait foi. Le sous-préfet a déjà apprécié le dossier et a délivré son autorisation sous conditions strictes de la loi N°90/055 du 19 décembre 1990 : respect de l'ordre public, responsabilité personnelle des organisateurs désignés. Pour l'avocat, revenir sur cette décision 24 heures après sur la base de simples allégations de "tensions internes" non étayées reviendrait à fragiliser l'autorité administrative elle-même. Au final, pour le camp de la direction intérimaire, la messe est dite : sauf élément nouveau caractérisé de trouble avéré à l'ordre public, la convention du 17 octobre à Odza se tiendra, comme prévu, dans le calme et la discipline. Cet article Cameroun-MRC : le récépissé du 28 septembre délivré, Willy Mengue tente de faire annuler la convention du 17 octobre est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

data.title: Cameroun-USA : Washington propose un nouveau chef de mission diplomatique à Yaoundé
data.description: © DR Selon la Maison-Blanche, le président Donald Trump a transmis au Sénat américain, le 28 septembre 2026, la liste de ses nominations diplomatiques. Y figure le nom de Christian Jové Ehrhardt comme prochain Ambassadeur extraordinaire et plénipotentiaire des États-Unis d'Amérique auprès de la République du Cameroun. Cette information, publiée sur le site officiel de la Maison Blanche et reprise par le Département d'Etat américain, est en attente de confirmation. Comme le veut la procédure américaine, le choix doit être validé par un vote du Sénat avant prise de fonction. A Yaoundé, le poste est vacant depuis le 17 janvier 2026, date du départ de l'ancien ambassadeur Christopher J. Lamora. Depuis, la mission est dirigée par le Chargé d'Affaires John G. Robinson. Déjà décoré par le Cameroun, ce n'est pas un inconnu à Yaoundé. Diplomate de carrière depuis 2007, Christian Jové Ehrhardt a servi au pas de Paul Biya et a été élevé au rang de Chevalier de l'Ordre de la Valeur en 2018. Originaire de New York, diplômé de la St. Lawrence University et du U.S. Naval War College, il parle couramment français et espagnol d'après sa biographie officielle du Département d'Etat. Son CV affiche des affectations sensibles : Algérie, Jamaïque, RCA, Soudan, Tchad, Haïti, Libye et Irak. Un profil lié aux dossiers migratoires Actuellement, il occupe le poste de Deputy Assistant Secretary au Bureau de la population, des réfugiés et des migrations (PRM) et dirige le Bureau de la remigration créé en 2025. D'après le Département d'Etat, c'est à ce titre qu'il a conduit en novembre 2025 une délégation américaine à Yaoundé, puis au Gabon et au Togo début 2026, pour discuter de coopération en matière de migration. S'il obtient le feu vert du Sénat, Christian Jové Ehrhardt hérite de trois dossiers brûlants : d’abord, finaliser l'accord migratoire. C'est son cœur de métier. Il est présenté comme l'architecte des protocoles d'entente signés en décembre 2025 entre Washington et Yaoundé sur l'accueil de ressortissants de pays tiers expulsés des USA. Sa mission sera de faire appliquer et d'étendre cet accord qui porterait sur 1 000 personnes pour 30 millions de dollars, malgré les polémiques révélées par le New York Times. Ensuite sécuriser les minerais stratégiques pour Washington. Le dialogue économique du 27 août 2026 a mis sur la table près de 7 milliards USD d'investissements américains : barrage de Grand Eweng (3 milliards), Grand aéroport du Littoral (2 milliards), et surtout le rutile et le projet de cobalt-nickel de Nkamouna dans la région de l'Est. Les USA veulent contrer la Chine sur les minerais critiques. Le lobbying autour de Nkamouna est déjà intense. Enfin, gérer l'après-AGOA. Le Cameroun est exclu de l'AGOA, mais ses exportations vers les USA ont explosé de 119% début 2026 (151,9 milliards FCFA). Il devra rassurer les milieux d'affaires camerounais tout en défendant la nouvelle doctrine commerciale américaine plus transactionnelle. Cet article Cameroun-USA : Washington propose un nouveau chef de mission diplomatique à Yaoundé est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .
